summary: The midterms complicate Trump's search for an Iran deal newspress_en Sat, 11/14/2026 - 04:00 Politics Democratic control of Congress will increase scrutiny of the war and its economic costs, but could also make the concessions needed for a lasting agreement with Tehran more difficult to deliver. ai.sum: Analysis argues that Democratic control of Congress after the midterms complicates Trump's search for an Iran deal.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Democratic midterm victory changes the political setting of the US war with Iran without necessarily ending it. A Democratic Congress will scrutinise the war's costs, funding and legal basis, but Trump, who faces no further election, may still prefer a deal he can present as a strategic achievement. The piece says a settlement would require sanctions relief, release of frozen assets and an end to the blockade, and that Congress could make permanent relief harder to deliver. It stresses that Iran's leverage lies in Hormuz, that Tehran's economy is under severe strain, and that the sequencing of concessions remains unresolved. The authors conclude that the White House may favour a narrower deal it can implement through executive waivers, even if this falls short of a lasting settlement.
brief.argument: The midterms make Congressional scrutiny of the Iran war more likely but could also make a lasting Iran deal harder to deliver, pushing Trump towards a narrower, executive-implemented arrangement.

Drawing on his expertise in medieval Russian literature, history, and folklore, he blends scholarly depth with compelling storytelling. His debut novel, Solovyov and Larionov , a literary detective novel set in Soviet-era…

ai.sum: Novelist Eugene Vodolazkin discusses technology and the human spirit in an interview on literature and culture.

brief.summary: In this interview with Al Majalla, Russian novelist and medievalist Eugene Vodolazkin argues that writers shape a people's collective memory more powerfully than historians, since readers keep Tolstoy's version of 1812 even after scholars corrected it. He sees history as a spiral rather than a closed circle, with progress confined to science and technology while the human soul stays the same. He holds that official history often serves present political needs, whereas creative works capture the spirit of an era. He values small sensory details that history drops, and argues that literature comes from gaps, forgetting and room for interpretation rather than from information. He presents his anachronisms in Laurus as symbols of a timeless eternity, and argues that machines can imitate a style but cannot become a writer, so only serious literature will resist AI. His central theme, he says, is time and mortality.
brief.argument: Literature and personal memory, not official history or information, shape how peoples understand their past and what it means to be human, while technology advances but the human spirit does not.

title: The mounting cost of airport hoax threats
summary: The mounting cost of airport hoax threats newspress_en Sat, 11/14/2026 - 03:54 Business & Economy Disrupting a flight does not necessarily require an explosive device, a weapon or even a perpetrator on the ground. Sometimes, an anonymous email claiming that explosives have been placed aboard a particular aircraft is enough to set off a long and costly chain of events in motion. The airport notifies the airline, the pilot is alerted, airspace is reorganised, and fighter jets…

ai.sum: Al Majalla examines the rising costs of airport hoax bomb threats, which can disrupt flights without any real device.

brief.summary: The authors argue that hoax bomb threats against flights are a cheap but highly effective form of economic sabotage, because the response (diversions, escorts, searches, crew timing breaches, missed connections, airport congestion) costs far more than the threat itself. They point to a November 2026 wave that hit dozens of European flights across at least nine countries, with no explosives found and no attribution established. They caution against quickly assigning political blame, especially amid European concern about Russian hybrid attacks, noting that motives could range from coordinated campaigns to copycats or individuals. They highlight a structural weakness: threats may be received in one country, aircraft cross a third country's airspace, and land in a fourth, so delays in assessing messages add cost. The piece stresses the need for better cross-border information sharing, which the EU activated after the wave.
brief.argument: Hoax airport threats are inexpensive to produce yet impose outsized economic costs, and their fragmented, multi-jurisdictional response exposes a structural weakness that should not be prematurely attributed to a hostile state.
recommendations: Strengthen cross-border information sharing for aviation-security threats
Avoid premature political attribution until investigations are complete
Speed up assessment of threat messages to cut decision-making delays

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Democratic midterm victory changes the political setting of Trump's Iran war without fully constraining his military choices. A Democratic Congress will scrutinise the war's costs, funding and legal basis, and could push for an end to the conflict. Yet it could also make a lasting deal harder to deliver, because permanent sanctions relief needs legislative cooperation. The piece stresses Iran's leverage over Hormuz and the economic pressure on Tehran, which has made the sequencing of concessions (blockade lifting versus reopening the strait) a central sticking point. It concludes that a deal relying mainly on executive waivers is more deliverable, but may fall short of Trump's goals and be vulnerable to a future administration.
